title: Macronutrients
text:
Human Body: Food We Eat › Macronutrients › Macronutrients — Revision note (part 1/1)

There are mainly five nutrients that combine together to form a healthy diet. They are mainly: Carbohydrates, Proteins, Fats, Vitamins and Minerals and Roughage and Water.

Among them Carbohydrates, Proteins, Fats are **Macronutrients**

) **Carbohydrates:**It provides energy to the body. These foods are called as **energy-giving foods.** Ex: Fruits such as Banana and apple, Potatoes and some cereals such as rice, wheat, maize, etc.

b) **Proteins:** These are the nutrients that help in the growth and repair of the body. It helps in building our muscles. Food rich in proteins are known as**bodybuilding foods. Ex**

**Pulses, Soyabean, Meat, Fish,Eggs, Milk and Milk Products.**

c) **Fats:**These nutrients provide energy to our body. It helps to keep our bodies warm.Ex: **Ghee and Butter**. Excess intake of fats results in its accumulation inside the human body making an individual obese.

[Figure 1]

title: Micronutrients
text:
Human Body: Food We Eat › Micronutrients › Micronutrients — Revision note (part 1/1)

**Vitamins and Minerals are required in smaller quantities hence micronutrients.**

**They are also called as protective foods.**

**Vitamins**: These nutrients protect our body from diseases to keep us healthy. A, B, C, D, E, K are different types of Vitamins. Vitamin A improves eyesight. Vitamin D is important for bones and teeth.

[Figure 1]

**Minerals:**These nutrients protect our body from diseases. Some of the examples of minerals are Calcium, Potassium, Iron, etc. They have different roles such as calcium is needed for formation of bones and teeth, iron is needed for formation of blood.

[Figure 2]

**Roughage :**The part of the food that cannot be digested by our body called roughage. It helps to remove waste material out of our body.

**Water:** It is important for digestion and is an essential part of the blood and other body fluids.

title: Balanced Diet and Food Preservation
text:
Human Body: Food We Eat › Balanced diet and food preservation › Balanced diet and food preservation — Revision note (part 1/2)

Food is an important energy source required by the human body for survival as well as for growth.

Proportionate intake of food is also very essential in order to maintain a nutrient balance in the human body.

There are different kinds of substances involved that contribute to keep an individual strong and healthy. These substances are defined as Nutrients.

**Functions of nutrients:**

1. They give us energy.

2. They are required for the growth of our body.

3. They help to repair our body and protects us from the infections.

[Figure 1]

**Balanced diet contains all nutrients in right amount including roughage and water.**

**Avoid Food Wastage:**

1. Take smaller servings

2. Store cooked food in refrigerator.

3. Share food with friends to avoid leftover food.

4. Raw and uncooked food should be kept in refrigerator to avoid spoilage.

5. We should avoid cooking large quantity food.

6. Vegtables and fruits should not be over exposed to air to prevent spoilage.

**Food Preservation:**

**a)** **Drying:**Grains are dried in the sun before storing. Onions and potatoes are kept in the open air in summer and then stored in a dry place.

[Figure 2]

**b)** **Boiling:**Milk is stored for a long time by either boiling or keeping it in the refrigerator.

[Figure 3]

**c)** **Adding preservatives:**Some of the substances when added to jams and pickles help them to preserve for a longer duration. These substances are called as preservatives**.**Oil, vinegar, salt, asafoetida ( _hing_ ), sugar are some preservatives.

[Figure 4]

**d)** **Cooling:**Refrigerator helps to keep fruits and vegetables fresh as they are kept at very low temperatures, so the microorganisms do not get the warmth that they need to grow.

[Figure 5]

title: Balanced Diet and Food Preservation
text:
Human Body: Food We Eat › Balanced diet and food preservation › Balanced diet and food preservation — Revision note (part 2/2)

**e)** **Canning/ Bottling:**When any kinds of foodstuffs are preserved in airtight containers, the micro-organisms are first destroyed, and it is ensured that water or air does not enter the foodstuff. It means that to preserve foods, the micro-organisms in them should be destroyed.

[Figure 6]

Human beings have two sets of teeth:

1) **Temporary (Milk teeth):**The first set of teeth is called temporary set or milk teeth. At the age of three, there is set of 20 teeth.

2) **Permanent:**Second set of teeth is called a permanent set of teeth.

According to shape and function, teeth are of four types:

a) **Incisors( four in each jaw)**

b) **Canines ( two in each jaw)**

c) **Premolars( four in each cavity)**

d) **Molars( six in each cavity)**

**Enamel:**It is the outermost layer of teeth. It is the hardest part of the teeth.

title: Excretory System
text:
Human Body: Digestive & Excretory Systems › Excretory system › Excretory system — Revision note (part 1/1)

**Excretory system**: The excretory system helps in removing wastes from our body.

**Organs of excretory system**: A pair of kidneys, ureters, urinary bladder and urethra make up the excretory system.

**Kidneys**: Formation of urine takes place inside the kidneys.

**Ureters**: Urine is transported through thin tubes from kidneys to the urinary bladder.

**Urinary bladder**: Urine is stored inside the urinary bladder.

**Urethra**: Urine is removed out of the body through the urethra.

**[Figure 1]**

**Healthy eating Habits**

1. We should wash our hands before and after meals.

2. Eat from a clean plate.

3. Chew slowly and properly.

4. Drink sufficient amount of water.

5. Do not drink water while eating, it dilutes the digestive enzymes.

6. Eat food rich in fibre.

7. We should eat balanced diet.

title: Digestive System
text:
Human Body: Digestive & Excretory Systems › Digestive system › Digestive system — Revision note (part 1/1)

**Digestion**: The process by which food is broken down into a simpler form so that it can be easily absorbed by our body is called digestion.

**Organs of the digestive system**: Mouth, food pipe, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, liver, rectum and anus are the organs of the digestive system.

**Mouth**: Digestion starts with the mouth. The teeth help to chew and break down the food. The mouth produces a fluid known as saliva that makes food softer and easier to swallow.

**Food pipe**: It passes food from mouth to stomach.

**Stomach**: The food is broken down further into smaller pieces by the churning process, inside the stomach.

**Small intestine**: It is a hollow and long, tube-like structure. Digestion is completed in the small intestine.

**Liver**: It produces digestive juices that help in digestion.

**Large intestine**: It absorbs water from the undigested food and forms waste product called faeces.

**Rectum**: It is the final part of the large intestine. Faeces are stored in the rectum for a short time.

**Anus**: Faeces get removed through the anus.

**[Figure 1]**

**Need for chewing food well and for regular bowel movements**

Digestion of carbohydrates starts in mouth, carbohydrates are digested first by salivary enzymes. If we do not chew our food properly digestion may slow down and feaces formation will not take place hence irregular bowel movement. So chewing food is very necessary. It keeps our digestion on track and keep us healthy.

**Need for Water**

1. Without water there is less absorption of food.

2. Digested food will dry up in the intestine without water.

3. Constipation and discomfort.

title: Parts of plant and their functions
text:
Plants in The Surrounding & Environment › Parts of plant and their functions › Parts of plant and their functions — Revision note (part 1/3)

Plants are one of the most important components of living things, as they provide us with food.

Other than providing oxygen, plants provide us with many other things such as wood, coffee, flowers, vegetables, etc.

A plant is divided into two parts- **the root and the shoot.**

**Root:**This part of the plant grows below the ground.

**Types of roots:**

**Taproot:** These types of roots grow below the soil from base to stem. Examples: carrot, radish, mango, and sunflower.

[Figure 1]

**Fibrous root:** These roots are the bunch of thin and bushy roots, and grow in soil together from base to stem. Examples: wheat, rice, and grass

[Figure 2]

**Functions of root:**

1. It provides support to the plants.

2. It absorbs nutrients and water from the soil that are essential for the growth of the plant.

**Shoot**: This part of a plant grows above the ground. It consists of leaves, stem, flowers, and fruits.

[Figure 3]

**Stem**: This is the main part of the plant. Some plants like banyan tree have a strong stem and are called as a trunk. Plants like pea and grapevine have weak stems and adhere to wall or stick for support.

**Functions of stem:**

1. They help to carry water and nutrients from root to leaves.

2. It helps the plant to stand upright.

3. Some stems are modified to store food and can be consumed. Ex: Potato, Ginger etc.

**Leaf**: Leaves act as a kitchen for the plant as it manufactures food for the plant. It grows on the stem. They have different shapes and sizes. Leaves are of varied colours but mostly they are found to be green. The different parts of a leaf are the**leaf blade, midrib and leaf stalk**.

[Figure 4]

Leaf-blade: It is the flat part of a leaf and is also known as the lamina.

Midrib: The vein passing through the centre of the leaf is known as midrib. It is responsible for the transportation of water and minerals to and from the leaf.

Leaf stalk: It is responsible to attach the leaf to a branch or a stem and is termed as petiole.

Stomata: The tiny pores present over the surface of the leaf is known as stomata. It is responsible for give and take of oxygen and carbon dioxide.

**Functions of leaves:**

1. They are responsible for preparing their own food with the help of a green coloured pigment called chlorophyll along with carbon dioxide and water in the presence of sunlight.

2. Leaves release oxygen, that is essential for living.

3. Leaves store food. For example, spinach, cabbage, lettuce are the leaves of plants that can be consumed.

**Flowers**: Flowers are bright in colour and have a pleasant smell. Flowers after development change into fruits. Fruits have one or more seeds, that grow into new plants

**Fruits**: Some fruits like mango and plum have one seed. While, fruits like apple, orange, lemon have few more seeds. Papaya and watermelon have many seeds. All fruits have different colour and taste. They also vary in shape and size.

**Seed**: Seeds grow into new plants. It has two types:

Monocot seeds: Some plants have only one cotyledon, as they do not store food. Examples: rice, maize.

[Figure 5]

Dicot seeds: Some plants have two cotyledons. They are fleshy and store food. Examples: pea, bean, and gram seeds.

[Figure 6]

**Photosynthesis:**

The process through which plants manufacture their own food using carbon dioxide, water, and minerals in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll is termed as photosynthesis.

**Transpiration:**

title: Terrestrial Plants
text:
Adaptation in Plants › Terrestrial plants › Terrestrial plants — Revision note (part 1/1)

**Habitat:** The place where a living organism lives in nature is called its habitat.

**Adaptations:** Features that help a plant or an animal to survive in its natural surroundings are called adaptations.

Plants show adaptations that are necessary for survival in a specific environment.

**Terrestrial plants:** Plants that grow on land are called terrestrial plants.

[Figure 1]

**Plants in plains:** Plains are large, flat areas of land.

**Adaptation: Trees growing in areas with low rainfall** have a lot of branches.

Most of the trees shed all their leaves during dry season therefore called deciduous trees.

Example: Mango, Ashoka, Gulmohar.

**Plants in areas with heavy rainfall**

Rubber and Teak are examples

They are evergreen trees.

They have many leaves.

**Adaptation in desert areas:**

The plants that grow in desert areas are adapted to conserve and store water.

The roots grow very deep in the sand to obtain underground water.

The leaves of the plants are modified into spines and thorns that decrease the loss of water.

E.g. Cactus, Babool

[Figure 2]

**Adaptation in mountains**

The trees are cone shaped.
The branches are sloping and the leaves are needle shaped.
The sloping branches and the leaves help in the sliding of snow from the leaves.

E.g. Pine, Fir, Deodar
[Figure 3]

**Plants in coastal areas**

Coconut tree.

Plants in coastal areas tolerate harsh conditions such as strong laden winds, poor and saline soils and rocky and sandy areas where it is very difficult for their roots to grow.

[Figure 4]

**Plants in swamps:**

Plants growing in swamps are called mangroves.

They grow in clayey soil. air cannot reach the roots of the above plants therefore they ave roots above soil. they are called breathing roots.

text:

Plants have roots fxed to the bottom. They are found in shallow water. Ex: Lotus and water lily.

They have flat and broad leaves

Their leaves have a waxy coating

Their stems are thin, long and hollow.

**Insectivorous plants:**Plants that feed on insects are called insectivorous plants.

title: Terrestrial Animals
text:
Adaptation in Animals › Terrestrial animals › Terrestrial animals — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Need for Adaptation**

In order to survive in slow changing environment animals need to adapt.

Animals also need to adapt in order to find food, water, air, shelter.

They also need to raise their young ones and protect them from predators.

**Adaptations in Terrestial Animals**

**Animals that live on land are called terrestial animals.**

• The place where a living organism lives in nature is called its habitat.
• Features that help a plant or an animal to survive in its natural surroundings are called adaptations.
• Animals show modifications in their body shape according to the environment and the food that they eat.
• Some of the modification seen in animals to adapt to their environment are

**1. Snow-covered regions:** Temperatures are always extremely cold in the polar regions.
• Animals have a thick coat of fur which helps them keep warm.
• Some animals have a layer of stored fat in their skin which helps to keep the body warm. Penguins have thick fat layer called blubber which helps them to keep warm.
• E.g. Polar bear, Yak
[Figure 1]

Some animals like hedgehogs go into winter sleep called **Hibernation.**

**2. Tropical rainforests:**Rainforests have a large cover of tall trees.
• Animals have tails, adhesive pads on their limbs, skin that camouflages with the surroundings, etc.
• Birds have a long beak to eat fruits.
• E.g. Red-eyed frog, monkey, etc.
[Figure 2]

title: Adaptation through modification of body parts
text:
Adaptation in Animals › Adaptation through modification of body parts › Adaptation through modification of body parts — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Adaptations according to feeding habits:** According to the feeding habits, animals have certain modifications or adaptations that help them to consume food.
**1) Herbivores:** The animals that consume plants are known as herbivores.
• Animals have teeth that are suitable to chew and grind plants.
• They do not have sharp teeth as they do not need to feed on animals for their food.
• Since they have to travel long distances in search of food, they have long and strong legs.
• E.g. Cow, camel, bullock, etc.
[Figure 1]
**2) Carnivores:**Animals that feed on other animals are known as carnivores.
• The teeth of the animal are modified so that they can tear the other animal.
• The canines are long, sharp, and strong that help them to tear the animal's skin and eat the flesh.
• Carnivorous birds have a strong, and sharp beak that helps them to tear the flesh of their prey.
• E.g. Lion, Tiger, Eagle etc.
[Figure 2]
**3) Omnivores:** Animals that can consume both plants and animals are known as omnivorous animals.
• The dentition is modified to consume both plants and meat.
• They do not have sharp canines but have broad molars and premolars.
• E.g. Humans, bears, etc.
[Figure 3]
**4) Parasites:**The animals that live either on the surface or inside the body of another organism is known as a parasite.
• The organism on which the parasite depends on for its nutrition is known as a host.
• They can cause damage to the host organism and in some cases kill the host organism.
• E.g. Bed bug, mosquito, liver fluke, etc.

[Figure 4]

title: Air Pollution
text:
Air › Air pollution › Air pollution — Revision note (part 1/1)

**Air Pollution:**

- Air pollution occurs when unwanted and harmful gases, dust particles, fumes or odour are introduced into the atmosphere in a way that makes it harmful to humans, animals and plants.

[Figure 1] [Figure 2]

**Causes of Air Pollution:**

- Air pollution is caused as a result of different human activities.
- Factories and industries release smoke and other harmful gases.
- Smoke released from burning of garbage and bursting crackers.
- Fumes from car exhausts contain dangerous gases.
- Heavy metals released by industries.
- Burning of solid wastes.

**Effects of Air Pollution:**

- Air pollution can make people sick.
- It becomes difficult to breathe and causes diseases such as lung cancer, respiratory and heart diseases.
- It can trigger an asthmatic attack (a respiratory infection).
- Some types of air pollution can cause harm to the ozone layer present in the atmosphere.

**Preventive measures**

- Industries should filter out harmful pollutants.
- Energy efficient boilers should be used.
- Industries should be away from residential areas.
- Less polluting fuel such as CNG should be used.
- Burning of garbage and wood to be avoided.

title: Change of State
text:
Materials & Solutions › Change of state › Change of state — Revision note (part 1/2)

**Matter:** Anything that has mass and occupies space is called matter.
• The three states of matter are solid, liquid, and gas.
Book, pen, pencil are solids. Water, milk, oil are liquids and oxygen, nitrogen, and water vapours are gases.

[Figure 1] [Figure 2]
**Change in the state:**
• When a substance is subjected to a change in temperature or pressure, the substance can undergo a change in the state of the matter.
• **Melting** is a process through which a solid can be converted into a liquid state by heating.
• Ice melts and changes into the water on heating.

[Figure 3]

**Other examples:** Melting of ice cream and candle wax.

• The process by which liquid changes into a gas is called **evaporation.**
• **Example:**Water evaporates and changes into water vapour form.
• Evaporation can be increased by providing heat to the liquid.
• Water can be converted into water vapour by **evaporation.**

[Figure 4]

• Rate of evaporation is slow at low temperatures but when we heat a liquid it becomes faster.

• The process by which a gas changes into liquid on cooling is called **condensation.**
• On cooling, water vapour changes into water.
• **Example:**Ice cold water in a glass left in open, water droplets are formed on the outer surface of the glass.

**Liquid to solid:**

• The process by which liquid is converted into a solid on cooling is known as **solidification**.

**Solution = Solute + Solvent**
• The substance in which the solute gets dissolved is known as the **solvent**.
• The **solute** is the substance that gets dissolved in the solvent.
• Water is known as a **universal solvent** as many substances get dissolved in water.
• A solute and solvent together make up the solution.

[Figure 1]
• If a substance gets completely dissolved in the solvent, the substance is known as **soluble substance**. E.g. Salt in water. A few gases such as oxygen, carbon dioxide, are soluble in water.
• If a substance does not completely dissolve in a solvent, the substance is known as an **insoluble substance**. E.g. Chalk powder in water. Gases that are insoluble in water are hydrogen, nitrogen, and helium.
• When two liquids are mixed completely without forming separate layers is known as**miscible liquids**. E.g. Alcohol in water.
• When two liquids do not mix completely and form two separate layers is known as **immiscible liquids**. E.g. Oil in water.
• When two immiscible liquids are mixed, the lighter liquid floats on the top of the heavier ones. So, when oil is dissolved in water, oil is lighter than water, therefore it starts floating in its surface.

The heavy and insoluble substances settle down at the bottom of the container. This process is called **sedimentation**.

title: Push & Pull
text:

**Push and pull:**

i. While pushing an object you hold the object and use your strength to move it forward. The object moves away from you. For example, closing a door.

ii. While pulling an object you hold it and use your strength to move it towards yourself. The object moves closer to you. For example, opening a door.

[Figure 1]

**Force as Push:**

Push is defined as the force that is responsible for an object to move from the state of rest away from the source of force.

### Examples of push:

- Pushing the trolley.
- Pushing of the car when it breaks down.
- Pushing the table from one place to another.

**Force as Pull:**

The pull is defined as the force that is responsible for an object to move from the state of rest but in the opposite direction when compared to the push i.e towards the source of force

### Examples of pull:

- Pulling the curtain.
- Dragging the box.
- Opening of the door.

**Force and its types:**

i. Force is a push or pull acting on an object.

ii. Force can move an object, stop a moving object, change the direction of movement of an object, and change the shape of an object. Force can be of many types, such a gravitational force, frictional force, magnetic force, and muscular force.

iii. The force that pulls every object downwards towards the centre of the Earth is called the force of gravity or gravity.

[Figure 2]

iv. The force that acts whenever any two objects rub together or come in contact is called frictional force or friction.

[Figure 3]

v. The force with which a magnet attracts certain metals, such as iron and nickel, towards itself is called magnetic force.

[Figure 4]

vi. The force exerted by the muscles to do work is called the muscular force. Running, walking all are examples of muscular force.
